A hands-on tour of the data feeding the Cape Nome district models, in the
same shape as the Tanacross and BC Golden Triangle data-exploration
notebooks: one section per layer, each with a rendered map, a note on what
the layer is and what it is for, and a note on how the model reads it. The
last sections turn to the outputs, the prospectivity surfaces and the
cross-validation numbers behind them.

This is a working notebook. It is not in `_quarto.yml` and is not linked
from the public site; it is the place to see every layer at once and
decide later what belongs in the public chapter and what belongs in a
deeper write-up.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import json
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import rioxarray

from ai_minerals.data._common import DATA_RAW, DATA_DERIVED

WORKING_CRS = "EPSG:3338"          # NAD83 Alaska Albers, the district grid CRS
NP = DATA_DERIVED / "nome_placer"
NG = DATA_DERIVED / "nome_geophys"
RM = DATA_RAW / "nome_mpm"
STRUCT = NG / "nome_structure_sharp" / "district_100m"

LODE_SERVED = NP / "mpm_lode_served" / "mpm_lode_served_district_3338.tif"
PLACER_SERVED = NP / "mpm_onshore" / "mpm_onshore_score_district_3338.tif"

print("district CRS:", WORKING_CRS, "(NAD83 Alaska Albers Equal Area)")
print("served lode raster present:  ", LODE_SERVED.exists())
print("served placer raster present:", PLACER_SERVED.exists())
```

```{python}
#| label: helpers
def _load(path):
    """Read a single-band raster to a masked float array + its 3338 extent."""
    da = rioxarray.open_rasterio(path).squeeze()
    arr = da.values.astype("float64")
    nod = da.rio.nodata
    if nod is not None and np.isfinite(nod):
        arr = np.where(arr == nod, np.nan, arr)
    arr = np.where(np.isfinite(arr), arr, np.nan)
    left, bottom, right, top = da.rio.bounds()
    return arr, (left, right, bottom, top)

def panel(ax, path, title, cbar_label, cmap="viridis", q=(2, 98),
          mask_neg=False, categorical=False, points=None, pcolor="#ff2d2d",
          psize=16, plabel="occurrences"):
    """Draw one raster on ax, optionally with occurrence points overlaid."""
    arr, extent = _load(path)
    if mask_neg:
        arr = np.where(arr < 0, np.nan, arr)
    if categorical:
        im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, extent=extent, origin="upper",
                       interpolation="nearest", aspect="equal")
    else:
        lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(arr, q)
        im = ax.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=lo, vmax=hi, extent=extent,
                       origin="upper", interpolation="nearest", aspect="equal")
    cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.82)
    cb.set_label(cbar_label, fontsize=8)
    cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    if points is not None and len(points):
        ax.scatter(points.geometry.x, points.geometry.y, s=psize, c=pcolor,
                   edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.35,
                   label=f"{plabel} (N={len(points)})")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.9)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, EPSG:3338)", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m)", fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    return arr, extent

def _ardf():
    return gpd.read_file(RM / "ardf_nome.geojson").to_crs(WORKING_CRS)

def _clip(g, extent):
    if extent is None:
        return g
    left, right, bottom, top = extent
    return g.cx[left:right, bottom:top]

def lode_36a(extent=None):
    """ARDF occurrences typed Cox-Singer 36a (low-sulfide Au-quartz vein)."""
    g = _ardf()
    g = g[g["model_code"].fillna("").str.contains("36a", case=False)]
    return _clip(g, extent)

def placer_occ(extent=None):
    """ARDF placer occurrences (commodity names placer, or model code 39x)."""
    g = _ardf()
    comm = (g["comm_main"].fillna("") + " " + g["comm_other"].fillna("")).str.lower()
    code39 = g["model_code"].fillna("").str.strip().str.startswith("39")
    g = g[comm.str.contains("placer") | code39]
    return _clip(g, extent)

def load_json(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
```

## The experiment

Two deposit types share this ground. **Placer** gold is the loose gold in
the gravels, the Nome beaches and creek bottoms that the 1899 rush was
built on. **Lode** gold is the hard-rock source: gold-bearing quartz
veins in the bedrock that the placer gold weathered out of and washed
down from. The project builds a separate prospectivity surface for each,
a map that ranks every cell in the district by how favorable it is for
that deposit type, trained on the recorded occurrences.

The ruler for both is the same. Every claim a model makes is checked
under leak-guarded spatial cross-validation: hold out whole regions of
the map, train on the rest, score the held-out occurrences, and pool the
out-of-fold predictions into a single area-under-the-ROC-curve (AUC). The
frame is presence/background: the positives are recorded occurrences, the
negatives are a sample of the district at large rather than known-barren
ground, so the model learns what separates occurrence sites from the
district average. The point of the discipline is to make a number mean
something before reporting it.

```{python}
#| label: headline
placer = load_json(NP / "mpm_onshore" / "mpm_onshore_presence_report.json")
gate = load_json(NP / "lode_structure_sharpen" / "lode_structure_sharpen.json")
boot = load_json(NP / "lode_groves_bootstrap" / "lode_groves_bootstrap.json")

groves = gate["datasets"][0]["arms"]["struct_groves"]["auc_gems"]
base = gate["datasets"][0]["arms"]["base"]["auc_gems"]
ci = boot["datasets"]["struct_groves"]["gems"]["ci95"]

print("PLACER (geomorphic terrain model, presence/background):")
print(f"  knowledge-overlay beach-line map : {placer['baseline_v31_composite_auc']:.3f}  (below chance)")
print(f"  terrain + geomorphology, spatial CV: {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_spatialCV_auc']:.3f}")
print(f"  terrain + geomorphology, buffered  : {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_buffered300m_auc']:.3f}")
print()
print("LODE (structure model on typed 36a labels, GeMS-mapped footprint):")
print(f"  base (terrain + geology + aeromag) : {base:.3f}")
print(f"  + Groves splay/intersection/fold   : {groves:.3f}  (gain +{groves-base:.3f})")
print(f"  bootstrap 95% CI on the gain       : [{ci[0]:+.3f}, {ci[1]:+.3f}]")
```

## Data layers

Each layer below is shown on the 100 m district grid (EPSG:3338), the
resolution the regional models run at. The native sources are finer (the
IfSAR elevation is 5 m, the LiDAR is 1 m); they are resampled to 100 m
here so every covariate sits on one grid.

### Terrain: IfSAR elevation, slope, and topographic position

```{python}
#| label: terrain
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
panel(axes[0], RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
      "IfSAR elevation (DEM)", "m above sea level", cmap="terrain")
panel(axes[1], RM / "ifsar_slope_district_3338.tif",
      "Slope", "degrees", cmap="magma")
panel(axes[2], RM / "ifsar_tpi_district_3338.tif",
      "Topographic position index", "TPI", cmap="RdBu_r")
plt.tight_layout()
```

**What it is.** The Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (IfSAR)
digital elevation model is Alaska's statewide 5 m radar elevation
surface. Slope and the topographic-position index (how high a cell sits
relative to its surroundings) are derived from it.

**What it is for.** Terrain is the backbone of the placer model: the
beaches, benches, and creek bottoms where placer gold concentrates have
distinct elevation and slope signatures. It is also the feature that made
the first lode model lie, because in a small box the lodes sit up in the
schist hills and the background sits down on the coastal flat, so a model
can separate them on elevation alone and never learn any geology. That
trap is the subject of the lode-results section below.

**How the model reads it.** Elevation, slope, and topographic position
enter both models directly as per-cell covariates.

### Geology: Nome Group units and the graphitic host

```{python}
#| label: geology
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
lodes = lode_36a()
panel(axes[0], NP / "covariates_mpm" / "geology_unit_code_district_3338.tif",
      "Surface geology unit", "unit code", cmap="tab20",
      categorical=True, mask_neg=True)
panel(axes[1], STRUCT / "struct_carbonaceous_host.tif",
      "Graphitic / carbonaceous host flag", "host present", cmap="cividis",
      points=lodes, plabel="36a lode")
plt.tight_layout()
```

**What it is.** The surface-geology unit at each cell, and a flag for the
graphitic (carbon-rich) schists of the Nome Group. The units come from
the statewide compilation; the graphitic-host flag comes from the
detailed Alaska state maps of the Seward Peninsula bedrock (DGGS SIM 3131
for the Nome and Solomon quadrangles, RI 2024-7 for Casadepaga), which
label the carbonaceous units explicitly.

**What it is for.** The Nome Group schists are the reactive host rock for
the gold-quartz veins. Orogenic gold of this type favors carbon-rich
units, the reactive-host control Groves et al. describe; the usual
explanation is that the wall-rock chemistry helps precipitate gold from
solution. The 36a lode occurrences (red) cluster on and near the
graphitic ground.

**How the model reads it.** The geology unit enters as a set of one-hot
indicator columns; the graphitic-host flag enters as its own binary
covariate.

### Structure: the fault sets, the named faults, and the Groves features

```{python}
#| label: structure
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
ext = None
for ax, fn, title in [
    (axes[0], "struct_dist_splay.tif", "Distance to a second-order splay"),
    (axes[1], "struct_dist_fault_intersection.tif", "Distance to a NE x NW fault intersection"),
    (axes[2], "struct_dist_fold_hinge.tif", "Distance to a fold hinge"),
]:
    arr, ext = panel(ax, STRUCT / fn, title, "metres", cmap="viridis_r")
lodes = lode_36a(ext)
for ax in axes:
    ax.scatter(lodes.geometry.x, lodes.geometry.y, s=14, c="#ff2d2d",
               edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.35, label=f"36a lode (N={len(lodes)})")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()
```

**What it is.** Three structural-distance fields, brighter where the
structure is nearer. A second-order **splay** is a small fault branching
off a main fault trunk; an **intersection** is where a northeast-trending
fault crosses a northwest-trending one; a **fold hinge** is the axis where
folded rock layers bend. All three are read from the most detailed public
structural map of the district, the Alaska state GeMS geodatabase for the
Nome mining district (DGGS PDF 94-39), which also names the district
faults: Anvil, Penny River, Aurora Creek, Charlie Creek, Boulder Creek,
Rodine.

**What it is for.** This is the lode model's centerpiece. Distance to the
nearest big fault, the obvious feature, is the wrong one for orogenic
gold. Groves and coauthors showed across many districts that the gold
does not sit on the fault trunks; it sits in the second-order splays, at
the intersection nodes, and near fold hinges, inside the reactive host.
Building those controls directly, rather than distance-to-any-fault, is
what separated the rebuilt lode model from the failed first version.

**How the model reads it.** Splay proximity, intersection proximity, and
fold-hinge distance enter as three covariates. The results section shows
that these are the three features the model leans on hardest, ahead of
any individual named fault.

### Geophysics: aeromagnetics and 1993 airborne resistivity

```{python}
#| label: geophysics
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
panel(axes[0], NP / "covariates_mpm" / "akmag_district_3338.tif",
      "Aeromagnetic field", "nT (stretched)", cmap="RdBu_r")
panel(axes[1], NG / "dighem1993" / "district_100m" / "dighem_res_log10_900hz.tif",
      "1993 DIGHEM apparent resistivity (900 Hz)", "log10 ohm-m", cmap="Spectral_r")
plt.tight_layout()
```

**What it is.** The regional aeromagnetic field (magnetic susceptibility
of the rocks) and the 1993 Nome DIGHEM-V helicopter electromagnetic
survey (DGGS GPR 2019-11, 400 m flight lines), reduced to apparent
electrical resistivity. The resistivity covers only the flown strip, so
much of the district is blank.

**What it is for.** The two geophysical layers part ways for the lode, so
it is worth separating them. The magnetics carry no independent lode
signal once you score them on the flown cells: the marginal AUC is
negative, not zero (about -0.02 in the central box, -0.06 district-wide),
and the apparent gain on the full extent is coverage, not geology. The
DIGHEM apparent resistivity is the one layer that helps at all, and only
a little: a small positive at district scale on the flown cells (marginal
AUC about +0.03), null in the smaller central box. Tested together the
two add about +0.06 in the central box, but the bootstrap interval grazes
zero in every case, and neither DIGHEM layer is in the served surface.
What carries the lode is structure, not geophysics (the Groves structural
features add +0.11 district-wide, P(Δ>0)=0.999).

An expected cross-check also failed. The graphitic units, predicted to
read as electrical conductors (a *low* apparent resistivity, the
alteration signature the literature looks for), instead read as more
resistive than their surroundings: median apparent resistivity about 0.3
to 0.8 log10 ohm-m higher across the 900 Hz, 7.2 kHz, and 56 kHz channels.
We did not test why. One untested possibility is that a 400 m airborne EM
survey over permafrost terrain does not resolve deep graphite, but we
cannot cite that, so it is a hypothesis, not a finding. Either way the
host flag earns its place as a map-geology covariate, not as a
geophysical conductor.

**What we did not build.** We tested these layers one at a time. We did
not construct the combined alteration index the literature advocates (low
magnetic susceptibility with low apparent resistivity and a localized
gravity low, read together as a proxy for a buried hydrothermal center),
and gravity is not in the Nome stack at all. The geophysics result here
is a limit of what we built, not a refutation of that index.

**How the model reads it.** The statewide aeromagnetic field enters the
served lode model as a base covariate, where it ranks low in feature
importance; on placer it is negative. The DIGHEM survey and gravity are
not in the served surfaces.

### Placer layers: the strandlines, the populations, and the LiDAR

```{python}
#| label: placer-layers
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
placers = placer_occ()
panel(axes[0], RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
      "Coastal terrain (placer setting)", "m above sea level",
      cmap="terrain", points=placers, plabel="placer occ", pcolor="#00d0ff")
panel(axes[1], NP / "beachline_rem" / "rem.tif",
      "Relative elevation model (1 m LiDAR, coastal strip)",
      "m above local base", cmap="RdYlBu_r")
plt.tight_layout()
```

**What it is.** The coastal terrain with the placer occurrences on it
(left), and a relative elevation model (right) built from the 2021
NOAA/USACE 1 m bare-earth LiDAR, which detrends the regional slope to
make low relief stand out. The Nome placers sit on a stack of raised and
submerged paleo-shorelines: the Second Beach at about +38 ft, the Third
Beach at +70 ft (the high-grade exemplar), the Fourth at +120 ft, and
several submerged stands offshore.

**What it is for.** These layers encode where the gold-bearing beaches and
their reworked stream placers are. The placer model is, in effect, a
beach-line model already: its existing features score nearness to a true
beach-stand elevation, the abrasion platforms, and the buried beach
lines. A round-2 test added the 1 m LiDAR strandline geometry and found
it added nothing measurable over that existing backbone, which says the
beach-line geometry was the model's spine all along. The 1 m LiDAR's real
value is berm-scale targeting on a single claim, not district-scale
ranking.

**How the model reads it.** The placer model carries explicit geomorphic
population features (beach, abrasion platform, buried beach, stream
reworking) on top of the terrain stack.

### Labels: the typed lode set and the placer occurrences

```{python}
#| label: labels
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
arr, ext = panel(ax, RM / "ifsar_dem_district_3338.tif",
                 "Recorded occurrences over district terrain",
                 "m above sea level", cmap="Greys")
lo = lode_36a(ext); pl = placer_occ(ext)
ax.scatter(pl.geometry.x, pl.geometry.y, s=18, c="#00b3ff", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.3, label=f"placer occ (N={len(pl)})")
ax.scatter(lo.geometry.x, lo.geometry.y, s=26, c="#ff2d2d", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.3, marker="^", label=f"36a lode (N={len(lo)})")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"36a lode occurrences shown: {len(lo)}   placer occurrences shown: {len(pl)}")
```

**What it is.** The training labels. The lode positives are the ARDF
occurrences the USGS classifies as Cox-Singer model `36a`, low-sulfide
gold-quartz vein, the deposit type the Nome lodes actually are. The placer
positives are the ARDF placer occurrences inside the area of interest.

**What it is for.** The typed lode set is the other half of the lode fix.
The first model used a keyword grab (anything tagged lode or vein), which
piled the positives into the two or three most-prospected spots. The 36a
type code is assigned from a deposit's own character, not its location, so
the positives disperse across the district and take the elevation
shortcut away. The headline label counts the models train on are 65
placer and 54 typed lode occurrences (48 of the lode set fall on
GeMS-mapped ground); the counts drawn here come straight from the ARDF
file and track those.

**How the model reads it.** Positives are the occurrence cells; negatives
are a background sample of the district. No occurrence-derived feature is
allowed to leak the label, which is the subject of the next section.

## How the algorithm consumes the data

The covariates above feed a random forest (300 trees, class-balanced,
fixed seed), but the modeling choice that decides whether the numbers mean
anything is the cross-validation, not the estimator.

```{python}
#| label: cv-scheme
sc = boot["scheme"]
print("Leak-guarded spatial cross-validation:")
print(f"  fold strategy     : {sc['fold_strategy']} regions")
print(f"  number of folds   : {sc['n_folds']}")
print(f"  block size        : {sc['block_size_m']:.0f} m  "
      f"(2x the {sc['variogram_range_m']:.0f} m residual-variogram range)")
print(f"  dead-zone buffer  : {sc['dead_zone_m']:.0f} m around every held-out point")
```

**Spatial blocks, not random folds.** Occurrences cluster, and nearby
cells share terrain, so a random train/test split lets the model score a
test point off its own near-neighbor in training. The folds here are
contiguous regions, sized from the range of spatial autocorrelation in
the model's own residuals (a variogram fit), so a held-out block is large
enough to be genuinely independent of the training ground.

**A dead-zone around every test point.** On top of the block split, any
training cell within 1 km of a held-out occurrence is dropped, which is
wider than the few-hundred-meter proximity buffers in the structural
features. A test point cannot be scored by a training neighbor sitting
just across the fold line.

**The leakage lesson.** An earlier experiment rasterized the knowledge
graph's occurrence-derived features onto the grid and saw the lode AUC
jump toward 0.97. That gain was a coverage artifact: the features and the
labels were drawn from one occurrence inventory, so a cell's own record
was informing its own prediction. Under a fold-aware leave-one-out, where
each held-out cell's own record is removed from the feature set, the gain
collapsed to roughly zero. Any feature derived from the occurrence
inventory is treated as guilty until cleared.

**Refit-on-all for the served map.** The AUC numbers are held-out
estimates of the pipeline's skill. The surface that gets served is the
same pipeline refit on all the labels, so it uses every occurrence to
draw the best map it can. The reported AUC describes the method's skill,
not a property of the all-data refit, and the two are kept distinct.

## Results

### The lode prospectivity surface

```{python}
#| label: lode-surface
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
arr, ext = panel(ax, LODE_SERVED,
                 "Served central-district lode favorability (struct_groves)",
                 "lode favorability (RF probability)", cmap="magma",
                 mask_neg=True)
lo = lode_36a(ext)
ax.scatter(lo.geometry.x, lo.geometry.y, s=22, c="#39ff14", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.4, marker="^", label=f"36a lode (N={len(lo)})")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()

v = arr[np.isfinite(arr)]
print(f"served cells: {v.size:,}   value range: [{v.min():.3f}, {v.max():.3f}]")
print(f"median: {np.median(v):.3f}   p90: {np.percentile(v,90):.3f}   "
      f"p99: {np.percentile(v,99):.3f}")
```

The served surface is masked to the GeMS-mapped footprint, the only ground
where the splay and intersection features are defined; outside it the
favorability is not meaningful, so it is left blank. The typed lode
occurrences (green) land on the high-favorability ground.

### Feature importance: the Groves controls lead, ahead of the named faults

```{python}
#| label: lode-importance
fi = gate["datasets"][0]["feature_importance_sharp_all_top12"]
names = [f[0] for f in fi][::-1]
imp = [f[1] for f in fi][::-1]
groves_feats = {"dist_splay", "dist_fault_intersection", "dist_fold_hinge"}
colors = ["#d1495b" if n in groves_feats else "#9fb1bd" for n in names]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.barh(names, imp, color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("random-forest feature importance")
ax.set_title("Lode feature importance (top 12) — Groves controls in red")
for i, (n, v) in enumerate(zip(names, imp)):
    ax.text(v + 0.002, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
```

The three Groves controls, splay proximity, fold-hinge distance, and
fault-intersection proximity, rank as the top three features, ahead of
every individually named fault and ahead of elevation. The structural law
the first model failed to find was real; the first model had the wrong
features for it.

### The lode mirage: restriction of range, and the fix

```{python}
#| label: lode-mirage
arms = gate["datasets"][0]["arms"]
groups = ["base\n(terrain+geology\n+aeromag)", "struct_groves\n(+ Groves controls)"]
inbox = [arms["base"]["auc_placer_core"], arms["struct_groves"]["auc_placer_core"]]
district = [arms["base"]["auc_gems"], arms["struct_groves"]["auc_gems"]]

x = np.arange(len(groups)); w = 0.36
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
b1 = ax.bar(x - w/2, inbox, w, label="in-box subset (placer core)", color="#e7a33e")
b2 = ax.bar(x + w/2, district, w, label="GeMS-mapped district (the gate)", color="#2e7d6b")
ax.axhline(0.70, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(1.45, 0.71, "0.70 gate", fontsize=8, ha="right")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(groups, fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-fold AUC"); ax.set_ylim(0.4, 1.0)
ax.set_title("Restriction of range: the in-box subset overstates skill")
for bars in (b1, b2):
    for r in bars:
        ax.text(r.get_x()+r.get_width()/2, r.get_height()+0.01,
                f"{r.get_height():.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
```

The in-box subset (the small box around the placer core) reads high for
every model, because inside it the lodes are upland schist and the
background is coastal flat. That is restriction of range: the model
separates the classes on the box geometry, not the geology. The
GeMS-mapped district AUC is the gate that strips the geometry out. The
first keyword-labeled lode model scored about `0.80` in the small box and
fell to `0.58` across the district, and for a while that collapse was the
chapter's negative result. The rebuild, typed dispersed labels plus the
Groves controls, brought the district number to `0.712`, a `+0.170` gain
over the same model without the structure features, with a paired
bootstrap 95% interval of `+0.108` to `+0.234` that clears zero.

### The peninsula generalization

```{python}
#| label: peninsula
pen = load_json(NP / "lode_peninsula_generalization" / "lode_peninsula_generalization.json")
cen = pen["central_matched"]["arms"]["struct_groves"]
wid = pen["wider"]["arms"]["struct_groves"]
east_ci = wid["bootstrap_east"]["ci95"]

bars = {
    "central district\n(mapped)": cen["auc_mapped"],
    "wider peninsula\n(mapped)": wid["auc_mapped"],
    "held-out east\n(Solomon/Council)": wid["auc_east"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
cols = ["#2e7d6b", "#2e7d6b", "#7b6cae"]
b = ax.bar(list(bars), list(bars.values()), color=cols)
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-fold AUC"); ax.set_ylim(0.4, 1.0)
ax.set_title("The Groves control generalizes to the wider peninsula")
for r in b:
    ax.text(r.get_x()+r.get_width()/2, r.get_height()+0.01,
            f"{r.get_height():.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"held-out east gain over base: +{wid['d_auc_east']:.3f}  "
      f"95% CI [{east_ci[0]:+.3f}, {east_ci[1]:+.3f}] (crosses zero)")
```

Rebuilt on regional bedrock maps and scored on lode occurrences dispersed
across the whole Seward Peninsula, the same splay-intersection-fold-host
signal predicts lodes at about `0.88` on the mapped ground, and at `0.82`
on an eastern cluster around Solomon and Council that the central model
never trained on. The control is not a central-district artifact.

A round-4 retest pinned down which part of that eastern signal travels.
With the eastern label set expanded by disciplined typing (eleven 36a
positives, up from nine) and the structure features split into two arms
scored against the same lithology-and-fault base, the orientation arm,
which resolves fault proximity into the northeast and northwest fault sets,
gains `+0.119` over the base in the east (95% CI `-0.008` to `+0.269`). The
Groves refinement arm, which instead carries splay and fault-intersection
proximity, does not travel: in the east it moves the AUC by `-0.047` over
the base, a 95% CI of `-0.189` to `+0.096` that spans zero. On the mapped
ground that same refinement is strongly positive (`+0.161`, CI `+0.093` to
`+0.227` in the central district; `+0.380`, CI `+0.302` to `+0.457` across
the peninsula). The reading is that fault orientation is the part of the
structural law that generalizes east, while the splay-and-intersection
refinement is tuned to the Nome district where it was built. That is why
the central-district surface is the served result and the peninsula
extension is reported as validated but provisional.

### The placer surface and the beach-line backbone

```{python}
#| label: placer-surface
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
arr, ext = panel(ax, PLACER_SERVED,
                 "Served placer favorability (geomorphic terrain model)",
                 "placer favorability (RF probability)", cmap="YlGnBu",
                 mask_neg=True)
pl = placer_occ(ext)
ax.scatter(pl.geometry.x, pl.geometry.y, s=18, c="#ff2d2d", edgecolor="black",
           linewidth=0.35, label=f"placer occ (N={len(pl)})")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"placer spatial-CV AUC: {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_spatialCV_auc']:.3f}   "
      f"buffered: {placer['mpm_geomorph_terrain_buffered300m_auc']:.3f}   "
      f"beach-line overlay: {placer['baseline_v31_composite_auc']:.3f}")
```

The placer surface is the one result here that held up on the first
careful try. The earlier knowledge-overlay map, a hand-built picture of
where the beaches run, scored `0.444` against the recorded occurrences,
below a coin flip, because it is a faithful map of the coastal beaches and
most of the recorded gold is up the creeks. The terrain-and-geomorphology
model that learns directly from the land scored `0.733` under spatial-block
cross-validation and `0.741` with a 300 m buffer. The buffered number
sitting above the unbuffered one is the reassuring direction: the result
is not an artifact of points leaking across fold boundaries. This surface
is the placer layer goldbug serves. (The colors here use a standard
high-is-bright scale; the live goldbug map applies its own styling.)

## Findings

**The same Nome Group veins source both maps.** The lode targets are the
fractured quartz-sulfide veins in the Nome Group schist; the placer gold
is what weathered out of those veins and was carried down. The genesis the
literature lays out is a three-stage system (the 1978 Alaska DGGS study of
the Nome coastal and offshore placers): glaciers stripped the mineralized
bedrock and dumped unsorted, low-grade till (about 70 ppb gold) across the
coastal shelf; marine transgressions then winnowed the fine matrix out of
that drift, leaving dense gold concentrated on a stack of raised and
submerged beach lines; late-stage streams cut across those beaches and
re-sorted them into the bonanza pay, Anvil Creek dissecting the Third
Beach being the type example. That is why the placer model is a beach-line
model and why the richest ground sits where streams cross old shorelines.

**The negative results are signal too.** Several things that looked
promising did not survive the ruler, and each one rules out a feature so
the next round does not re-try it:

- Splitting the faults out by name **hurt** the lode model (the per-named-fault
  arm scored `0.422` against the lumped Groves arm's `0.712`). Orientation
  and structural role beat fault identity.
- The deposit-scale Albion fault at Rock Creek was **redundant** once the
  splay and intersection bands were in (it moved the AUC by `-0.021`,
  within noise).
- The drift-on-beach lever is a **tested null**. The raised-beach model
  holds that gold concentrates where a strandline crosses gold-bearing
  glacial drift. The most precise Nome-town surficial map (USGS MF-247)
  maps the coastal plain as one undifferentiated unit, so the one
  digitizable line is the bedrock/Quaternary contact, a proxy for the
  drift's inland edge. As a covariate it adds nothing over the beach-line
  base (strandline-crossing marginal AUC `-0.030`, 95% CI `-0.072` to
  `+0.011`), and the positives sit a median 1.6 km seaward of the contact.
  Whatever the drift contributes is already inside the beach-line score.
  This is a null for the proxy, not a refutation of the mechanism: a
  discrete central-Nome drift polygon, if one is ever digitized, could
  still carry more.
- **Typing the placer positives by coastal population was a null, set by
  sample size.** Only 8 of the 65 recorded placer occurrences are cleanly
  typed as coastal beaches (5 abrasion-platform, 3 strandline, after
  Hudson 2006 and Metcalfe & Tuck 1942); the other 57 are upland
  stream-and-gulch placers or district-wide composites. Both coastal types
  sit farther from the lodes than the district background, not nearer, and
  the two are indistinguishable on every local-source covariate tested
  (every rank `p >= 0.29` at n = 5 versus 3). The one direction matching
  the local-source hypothesis, abrasion-platform sitting nearer the
  lode-belt axis than strandline, does not reach significance (`p = 0.11`).
  The real local-source structure is the upland placers sitting on their
  own lodes (median 1.4 km), which is partly circular and already captured
  by terrain, so the pooled model gains nothing from a distance-to-lode
  feature (`+0.026`, CI `-0.020` to `+0.071`). A powered retest needs a
  positive set with more typed coastal beaches: the Metcalfe & Tuck
  paystreak inventory or the NovaGold drill database.
- The 400 m **aeromagnetics carried no independent lode signal** on the
  flown cells (marginal AUC about -0.02 to -0.06). The DIGHEM **apparent
  resistivity** helped a little at district scale (about +0.03) but not in
  the central box, and neither DIGHEM layer is in the served surface. The
  predicted graphitic-conductor cross-check failed the other way: the
  graphitic units read as more resistive, not less. We did not build the
  combined low-magnetic / low-resistivity / gravity-low alteration index
  the literature advocates, so this is a limitation, not a refutation.

**What each layer contributed.** Terrain carries the placer model and set
the trap for the first lode model. Geology supplies the host. Structure,
specifically the Groves splay/intersection/fold features, is what moved
the lode from chance to a real number. Of the geophysics, the magnetics
did not help and the resistivity helped only marginally; structure, not
geophysics, carries the lode. The typed `36a` labels were half the lode
fix, the Groves features the other half.
